title: Ether.fi Moves Payments Stack onto MoonPay Infrastructure
snippet: The self-custodial neobank will use MoonPay's ramps, virtual accounts and cross-chain trading to deliver a single-verification payments experience. The post Ether.fi Moves Payments Stack onto MoonPay Infrastructure appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Ether.fi, the self-custodial crypto neobank reporting more than $6 billion in assets under management, has announced a partnership that will move its entire payments infrastructure onto MoonPay‘s integrated stack. The deal covers fiat onramps and offramps, cross-chain trading, institutional-grade virtual bank accounts and crypto deposits, all without requiring users to surrender control of their private keys.

The announcement was made on 6 October 2026. MoonPay, which says it serves more than 35 million customers across 180 countries and holds regulatory licences in multiple jurisdictions including the United States, will supply four products: Headless Ramps, which embed fiat entry and exit flows natively inside the ether.fi app without redirects; MoonPay Trade for cross-chain routing and asset conversion; MoonPay Enterprise for virtual bank accounts supporting ACH, Fedwire, SWIFT, Faster Payments, SEPA and Open Banking rails; and MoonPay Crypto Deposits for inbound transfers from external wallets and centralised exchanges. The four products will roll out progressively to ether.fi’s user base over the coming months.

The structural problem being solved

Rok Kopp, co-founder and chief growth officer of ether.fi

The core friction the partnership targets is well known in self-custodial product design. Where a traditional neobank can bundle its card, bank account and funding flows through a single compliance check, a self-custodial platform has historically been forced to source those functions from separate vendors. The result is that users face repeated identity verification steps, and the transaction experience breaks at the handoff between the app and an outside provider. Ether.fi and MoonPay say that by consolidating onto one infrastructure layer, a user completes verification once and that credential carries across products, subject to local regulatory requirements.

Rok Kopp, co-founder and chief growth officer of ether.fi, framed the benchmark clearly: “The bar for ether.fi isn’t other crypto products. It’s whatever banking app a user opens every morning. Every integration we make is measured against that standard.”

Spending data and market positioning

The release includes transaction data attributed to Paymentscan, an on-chain card-tracking service. According to those figures, ether.fi card users spent $123.7 million across 1.5 million transactions in September 2026, up from $24.1 million in the same month a year earlier, a more than fivefold increase. Since launching in April 2025, cumulative card spend is reported at $918.1 million across 11.6 million transactions. The company says card volume growth has been largely uncorrelated with bitcoin price movements over the same period, citing months in which its volume rose while bitcoin fell by double digits.

The third-party source for that data, Paymentscan, is not a widely cited industry benchmark, so the figures should be treated as company-provided rather than independently verified. Editors may wish to seek corroboration before publishing them as established facts.

Regulatory read-across

The regulatory architecture underpinning the partnership is worth noting. Ether.fi’s self-custodial model means it does not hold user funds in the way a licensed deposit-taking institution would, which has historically allowed it to expand across markets without obtaining a banking licence in each jurisdiction. MoonPay’s licensed fiat-rail infrastructure handles the regulated perimeter. That division of labour is commercially efficient but sits under intensifying scrutiny. In the EU, MiCA’s stablecoin and crypto-asset service provider frameworks impose new obligations on entities facilitating fiat-to-crypto flows, and the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority is advancing its own cryptoasset registration and market regime. How the compliance boundary between Ether.fi and MoonPay is drawn will matter as those frameworks come into force.

The broader embedded-finance and digital-asset payments segment is crowded, with several infrastructure providers competing for neobank integration contracts. MoonPay’s differentiation here rests on the breadth of its licensed coverage and the unified KYC layer, which removes the multi-verification problem that has blunted rival self-custodial products. Whether the single-verification promise holds in practice across all supported jurisdictions will be the commercial test.

title: Late Payments Trap £26bn in Unpaid Invoices, Hitting 1.5m UK Firms
snippet: New analysis from Century Business Finance links overdue invoices to 14,000 UK business closures annually and an £11bn drag on the economy. The post Late Payments Trap £26bn in Unpaid Invoices, Hitting 1.5m UK Firms appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Late payments remain a structural threat to UK small business survival, with an estimated £26 billion locked in overdue invoices at any one time, according to new analysis published by loan broker Century Business Finance. The firm’s research, drawn from Office for National Statistics, Companies House and government datasets, finds that around 1.5 million UK businesses, or 28% of the small business population, are affected by late payments each year.

The headline figure the report places on the problem is stark: late payments are estimated to contribute to approximately 14,000 business closures annually, equivalent to 38 companies ceasing operations every day. The aggregate cost to the broader UK economy is put at almost £11 billion per year.

The behavioural trap

Ben Larkins, co-founder of Century Business Finance

Perhaps the most telling finding is not the scale of overdue debt but the reluctance to recover it. One in three small businesses does not formally pursue late payments, the analysis found, citing a desire to protect customer relationships. That dynamic is well understood in trade credit markets but rarely quantified at this level: the fear of losing a client routinely outweighs the financial damage of carrying unpaid invoices, at least until the cash position deteriorates sharply.

Ben Larkins, co-founder of Century Business Finance, said: “Late payments aren’t just frustrating, they can prevent otherwise healthy businesses from paying staff, covering day-to-day costs or investing in future growth. Allowing unpaid invoices to build up often creates much bigger financial pressures in the long run.”

Century also published a regional breakdown using late-payment incidence rates from the Q1 2026 Business Health Report published by insolvency trade body R3, scaled against SME population data. The West Midlands recorded the highest rate at 2,625 late payments per 100 SMEs, followed by Scotland at 2,135 and Yorkshire and Humber at 1,373. Greater London, often assumed to carry the heaviest commercial stress, ranked sixth at 1,138 per 100 SMEs. Northern Ireland recorded the lowest rate at 431.

Regulatory and market context

The late-payments problem sits against a backdrop of intermittent government attempts to tighten the regime. The UK Prompt Payment Code, administered through the Small Business Commissioner, sets a 30-day payment standard for public sector contracts and a 60-day ceiling for the private sector, but compliance and enforcement have long been criticised as inadequate. Successive consultations have discussed mandatory reporting, stronger penalties and extending the Commissioner’s powers, but legislative progress has been slow.

At the product level, the gap between the scale of overdue trade receivables and the availability of invoice finance remains commercially significant. Invoice factoring and asset-based lending are established tools, but adoption among micro and small enterprises is limited, partly due to cost and partly due to unfamiliarity. Open finance infrastructure, which in principle allows lenders to assess receivables and cash-flow data in near real time, creates the conditions for more granular, dynamic working-capital products. Several UK fintechs and challenger banks have moved into embedded invoice-finance rails, though penetration among businesses below the £1 million revenue threshold remains modest.

Century Business Finance has also launched a free SME Cash Flow MOT tool alongside the research, a self-assessment resource the company says helps businesses evaluate their financial health and prepare for growth. The firm operates as a loan broker rather than a direct lender, connecting SMEs with funding of between £10,000 and £250,000 from its panel of lenders.

The research is self-commissioned and serves as a marketing exercise for the broker. The underlying datasets it cites, ONS business population estimates and Companies House insolvency data, are publicly available and reputable, but the causal link between late payments and the 14,000 closure figure is an estimate rather than a direct attribution from official statistics.

title: Etraveli Group Rebrands Precision as Standalone Travel Fintech Arm
snippet: The Stockholm flight-tech group is repositioning Precision from a risk tool into a dedicated fintech business serving airlines and OTAs. The post Etraveli Group Rebrands Precision as Standalone Travel Fintech Arm appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Etraveli Group has formally rebranded Precision, previously known primarily as an internal risk management solution, as the group’s dedicated travel fintech division. The repositioning, announced on 6 October 2026, broadens Precision’s scope beyond fraud controls and gives it a commercial identity as a standalone B2B fintech provider serving airlines, online travel agencies and global travel businesses.

Peny Rizou, chief fintech officer of Etraveli Group and head of Precision

The refreshed Precision launches with two named products. Precision Fraud Prevention uses machine learning models trained on travel-specific transaction data to help clients approve a higher proportion of legitimate bookings while containing fraud losses. Precision Travel Flexibility is a decisioning layer that allows travel companies to offer contextual cancellation and change options, adjusting eligibility and pricing at the individual booking level to lift attachment rates and protect margin. Etraveli says both products are designed around the structural realities of the travel sector, notably thin margins, high cancellation volumes and significant exposure to card-not-present fraud.

Peny Rizou, chief fintech officer of Etraveli Group and head of Precision, framed the move as an external commercialisation of capabilities developed over two decades of internal use. “Over two decades, we have honed these capabilities internally. By evolving Precision into a specialised fintech arm, we are giving airlines, OTAs and travel partners access to travel-native intelligence that turns challenges like fraud and cancellation risks into scalable, profit-generating strategies.”

Precision already has named distribution relationships with Outpayce by Amadeus, Mastercard Gateway, Sabre and Checkout.com, which collectively represent substantial coverage of the global flight booking and payments infrastructure. Etraveli did not disclose revenue attributable to Precision, nor the split between internal group usage and third-party client contracts.

Market context

The travel payments and fraud-prevention segment has attracted growing fintech interest as airlines and OTAs look to recover margin lost to high chargeback rates and the operational cost of flexible ticketing rules introduced widely during the pandemic period. Several specialist vendors, including Forter, Signifyd and Riskified, already compete in the transaction-level fraud decisioning space across verticals. Precision’s stated differentiation is domain specificity: models trained solely on travel data rather than cross-vertical datasets, which the company argues improves approval accuracy for the irregular purchase patterns typical of flight bookings.

The Travel Flexibility product places Etraveli in a narrower but expanding category. With regulators in the EU and UK maintaining or tightening consumer rights around flight disruption, airlines face commercial pressure to package flexibility as an upsell rather than absorb it as a liability. A decisioning layer that prices and distributes those options dynamically carries revenue-share potential that fraud tooling alone does not.

Competitive positioning

Etraveli’s structural advantage is captive transaction volume. The group processes flight bookings for Booking.com, Google Flights, Skyscanner and Kayak, and operates its own consumer OTA brands including Gotogate and Mytrip. That proprietary data estate underpins the machine learning claims in a way a pure-play vendor without comparable volume cannot easily replicate. However, the durability of that advantage depends on whether Precision can demonstrate model lift over general-purpose fraud tools to external clients who already have incumbent vendor relationships.

Etraveli is backed by CVC Capital Partners and KKR. It employs more than 3,200 people across 11 offices and serves over 48 million travellers annually in more than 75 markets. The group did not indicate whether Precision is being positioned for a separate capital raise or eventual spin-out, nor whether the repositioning is accompanied by any change in headcount or cost structure within the division.

title: Solaris Adds Instant-Access Savings Account to ADAC Credit Card Range
snippet: The Berlin-based BaaS bank is rolling out a Tagesgeldkonto to ADAC cardholders, offering a 3.5% promotional rate for three months before reverting to The post Solaris Adds Instant-Access Savings Account to ADAC Credit Card Range appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Solaris, the Berlin-headquartered Banking-as-a-Service provider, has added an instant-access savings account to the ADAC credit card portfolio, extending a partnership that has grown steadily since Solaris took on the programme. The product, known in Germany as a Tagesgeldkonto, follows a soft launch in September that made it available to 50,000 ADAC cardholders ahead of the full portfolio rollout.

Steffen Jentsch, CEO at Solaris

The account sits alongside the existing credit card account and can be opened digitally in a few steps. Onboarding requires IBAN linking and two-factor authentication. Deposits and withdrawals are processed either via the ADAC credit card account or a designated reference account, and deposited funds remain available daily.

Joost Greve, managing director of ADAC Finanzdienste GmbH

At launch, new customers receive a promotional interest rate of 3.5% per annum for the first three months. After that, a variable standard rate of 1.5% per annum applies to balances up to 100,000 euros. Interest accrues monthly and can be tracked daily through the ADAC credit card app and online banking portal.

Steffen Jentsch, chief executive of Solaris, said the savings product was the “next logical step” in the partnership, with a stated aim of continuously expanding digital services for ADAC’s large membership base. Joost Greve, managing director of ADAC Finanzdienste GmbH, pointed to simple digital processes and security standards as the product’s defining priorities.

Expanding the embedded product suite

The savings account is not the only feature added to the ADAC card this year. Since May, cardholders have had access to a function called EuroAbruf, which allows customers to transfer up to 5,000 euros from their available credit limit directly to a personal bank account via SEPA Instant Credit Transfer. The process is fully self-service and subject to risk and authorisation checks. According to a survey cited by Solaris, 90.3% of participating cardholders said they were very satisfied with the additional card features, though the methodology and sample size were not disclosed.

The two additions together represent a pattern familiar in embedded finance: a card product used as a distribution anchor, with savings, credit access and payments layered progressively on top. This approach deepens the cardholder relationship and increases product revenue per user without requiring a full banking app relaunch.

Market and regulatory context

Solaris holds a full German banking licence, which gives it the regulatory standing to offer deposit-taking products directly rather than relying on a separate bank partner. That distinction matters in a sector where several BaaS competitors operate as technology layers over a licensed bank, creating additional counterparty risk and compliance complexity. The German deposit guarantee scheme (Einlagensicherungsfonds) applies to deposits held at Solaris, which will be relevant to any ADAC cardholder weighing the savings product against alternatives.

The competitive backdrop for BaaS-embedded savings is also developing quickly. Across Europe, several embedded-finance platforms and challenger banks have introduced savings products as a means of widening net interest margin, particularly at a time when central bank rate cycles have made deposit economics more attractive than they were for most of the low-rate decade. The promotional rate of 3.5% positions the ADAC product above the standard variable rate but below the leading easy-access rates available on the open market from specialist savings platforms, meaning ADAC cardholders who are already inside the app ecosystem are the primary target rather than active rate-shoppers.

The next milestone to watch is whether Solaris and ADAC Finanzdienste extend the product set further, potentially into investment or lending products, as the embedded suite deepens.

title: How agentic payments present risk
snippet: “There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate,” writes one financial services consultant. “That's a problem for issuers as they contemplate making credentials available to AI tools.”
fullText:
Aaron Cheiffetz is an analyst and executive strategist in the financial services industry, working with banking leaders on artificial intelligence governance, enterprise architecture, regulatory compliance and operational resiliency. He is based in Charlotte, North Carolina.

In the debit-card context, Regulation E generally limits a consumer's liability for unauthorized transfers involving a lost or stolen debit card to $50 if the loss is reported within two business days. But Regulation E excludes from its definition of an “unauthorized electronic fund transfer” a transfer initiated by a person to whom the consumer furnished the access device, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that transfers by that person are no longer authorized. 

The official commentary goes further: if a consumer furnishes an access device and grants another person authority to make transfers, the consumer can remain liable even when that person exceeds the authority given. Regulation E defines "person" to include both natural persons and organizations, including corporations. 

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Aaron Cheiffetz

What it doesn't say is how that rule applies when credentials are furnished to software operated by a company. A January research report by the Consumer Bankers Association asks whether sharing credentials with an AI tool could trigger this exclusion and leave the consumer responsible for the agent's mistakes.

In the credit-card context, the Truth in Lending Act, implemented by Regulation Z, provides a similar unauthorized-use framework that turns on whether another person had actual, implied, or apparent authority to use the account. Here too, it's unclear how that rule applies when an AI tool acts on a cardholder's behalf.

Visa and Mastercard have zero-liability policies for unauthorized transactions that go beyond federal law. But those policies still depend on a transaction being classified as unauthorized. They don't clearly resolve what happens when a consumer authorized an agent to transact but disputes whether a particular purchase fell within the scope of that authority. 

These are the kinds of issues that should be addressed in agentic payment frameworks, which Mastercard and Visa are developing. Such frameworks envision the payment system recording or validating instructions given by users to agents and taking steps to make sure agents and merchants are who they purport to be and that transactions remain consistent with the consumer's mandate. 

But a host of questions remain. There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate. That's a problem for issuers as they contemplate making credentials available to AI tools. 

Where risks aren't adequately addressed and priced, issuers may be tempted to act defensively by agreeing to credential-sharing only with sophisticated AI-tool providers under negotiated contracts, adopting onerous identity-confirmation processes, or refusing transactions in some circumstances. All of this would tilt the playing field in favor of incumbent platforms.

Some clarity about liability for unauthorized transactions will be important before agentic payments are rolled out more broadly. Voluntary efforts by banks and payment networks won't go far enough to assuage concerns. More fundamental issues of consumer liability need to be addressed. 

At minimum, three things need to happen. 

First, laws should distinguish between a consumer’s own acts and the acts of others, including AI tools acting on a consumer's behalf. Second, when consumers give others authority to initiate financial transactions, the parameters of that authority, such as amounts, merchants, timing, and other limits, should be documented in a form the payment system can use. Third, the allocation of losses among issuers, payment networks, merchants, and AI-tool providers should not be an issue for consumers.

Firms crack down on money mules but need to do more

              

  

  

  
    

    

      

Financial firms are shutting down hundreds of thousands of suspected money mule accounts, but organised criminal groups are still shifting dirty money through multiple bank accounts before cashing out.

  

            						

An FCA survey found firms have closed an increasing number of suspected mule accounts over the last 3 years: 238,396 suspected mules had their accounts closed in 2025, up from 184,935 in 2023 and 233,269 in 2024.

An increase in account closures could reflect broader customer growth alongside improvements in identifying and acting on suspected mule activity, rather than necessarily meaning mules make up a higher proportion of firms’ business.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates more than £100bn is laundered through the UK or UK corporate structures each year. Money mule activity is one way criminals move these funds, by using people’s bank accounts to receive or transfer money on their behalf.

Account closures were highest among customers aged 26 to 39 (91,073), while the sharpest increase was among customers aged 40 to 49 (37,274 in 2025 up from 25,760 in 2024). Customers aged 25 and under (85,425) also represented a significant proportion of closures.

The financial regulator also found evidence that criminals moved fraudulent funds through multiple accounts, usually cashing out between the second and fifth account. By this stage, payments are harder to detect and trace, and shows that firms need to crack down on activity as early as possible.

Some accounts had been used repeatedly for mule activity before firms shut them down and had also been used for fraud. This points to an established criminal infrastructure rather than opportunistic, isolated incidents.

The FCA, NCA, Home Office, the Treasury and industry are leading on 9 system priorities (PDF) as part of the UK’s response to economic crime. The FCA is playing a key role on the money mules priority by working with industry on an action plan to tackle the problem, including better ways for firms and law enforcement to share intelligence on suspected money mule activity.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Money muling is a crime and it's not victimless. It makes it harder to recover stolen cash and helps criminals move and hide the proceeds of serious offending. People should be wary of contact out of the blue, including via online channels, asking them to funnel money through their account as they could face prosecution.

'It's good that financial firms are taking action on mules, but banks, law enforcement, technology companies and consumers all have a role to play in stopping people being drawn into criminal activity.'

  

Money mule warning signs to look out for

If you’re approached out of the blue online with an offer of quick cash, then alarm bells should ring.  

Scammers may call it a 'job offer' but no legitimate company will ask you to use your own bank account to transfer their money.  

Never give sensitive financial details to someone you don’t know and trust.

Be aware that the consequences of becoming a money mule could include losing access to your bank account and possible prosecution. 

Find out more about money transfer scams.

Notes to editors

Read our multi-firm review: Money mules: mule activity and cashing out findings.

Alongside the National Economic Crime Centre, the FCA is alerting firms to its latest findings.

Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA’s strategic priorities (PDF).

The FCA surveyed 35 retail banks, building societies, challenger banks, payment institutions and e-money institutions.  

The FCA also established a public/private cell in 2025 – a working group with 22 regulated firms. The cell looked at 140 cases, covering 7 types of fraud.

The FCA found card payments were the most common cash-out method and used to make lots of low-value transactions, or higher-value payments to local businesses and retailers. This can resemble legitimate consumer spending and be harder for firms to detect.    

Retail banks accounted for most transactions passing through mule accounts, whereas other firms experience lower volumes but higher-value transactions. This suggests different criminal behaviours, cash-out strategies and risk concentrations. 

The Home Office’s Fraud Strategy 2026 to 2029 recognises the role that money mule networks play in facilitating fraud and financial crime.

This work follows previous publications on detecting and preventing money mules, and firms' use of the National Fraud Database (NFD) and money mule detection tools.

title: Stablecoin startups advance payments
snippet: Entrepreneurs embracing the digital assets are pushing payments modernization forward, and bringing incumbents along too.
fullText:
Fintech entrepreneurs are using stablecoins as a means of breaking into the payments industry and driving digital modernization.

Startups such as MassPay and Rain have been forging new pathways for payments that embrace stablecoins, either incorporating or bypassing aging rails. They see an expansive opportunity ahead as they begin to make inroads.

While traditional payments players, including card network giant Visa and mega processor Fiserv, have also glommed on to the stablecoin trend, their legacy infrastructures may increase the difficulty of adapting to digital schemes.

Meanwhile, younger companies are amassing capital from venture investors and hiring employees to build stablecoin networks and accessories. The appeal for investors has been a simple one, according to Verda Ventures General Partner Alex Witt.

“The basic premise behind our fund is: sending payments should be as easy, fast, and cheap as sending a text message,” Witt said in an interview this month. “We fundamentally believe with blockchain, mobile phones, and the internet, that is completely possible.”

Witt and his business partner, Amit Chu, created a venture fund two years ago to invest in stablecoin startups and it has since drawn $40 million, he said, allowing the fund to purchase minority stakes in about two dozen companies globally. 

It’s a real change from when Witt first started to raise money for the fund in 2024 and people thought he was “completely crazy,” he said.

The Verda portfolio includes the fintech Yellow Card focused on payments in Africa as well as the blockchain infrastructure services company Capa, which operates in Latin America.

Two other companies the fund invested in have already been sold, specifically Kulipa and Beam. In addition, digital processor Stripe is circling another possible purchase, Witt said, declining to name it.

Rain evolves into stablecoin services

Rain’s holding company, Signify, began as a different business and then morphed into the one branded as Rain today. It has collected about $338 million in equity investments along the way, according to a spokesperson for the company. 

Among the private company’s investors are San Francisco investment firm Iconiq Capital, Sapphire Ventures and Coinbase’s former chief technology officer, Balaji Srinivasan, with a quarter of a billion dollars raised in the most recent round disclosed in January.

Rain provides stablecoin infrastructure services that enable corporate customers to bridge stablecoin payments so that money can move from the digital assets to traditional payment rails. Corporate clients embed the technology in their services for consumer use, letting consumers tap stablecoins in a way that’s less invisible to users. 

Early clients were crypto firms, fintechs and neobanks, sometimes in countries where the digital assets acted as a hedge against inflation, such as in Argentina. But then Rain began attracting bigger names, landing remittance provider Western Union as its first major customer last year, then a large peer, MoneyGram, and ticketing company Live Nation followed this year.

This week, Rain said it’s making a digital wallet available to consumers that will enable them to save, spend and send from a stablecoin balance that is backed by cards the company issues. For now, consumers will still custody their funds with the non-custodial wallets, but the company plans to offer custodial wallets by yearend.

Rain expands following Genius Act

Rain has grown by acquisition too. In August, Rain purchased the California payments and technology firm Ansa for an undisclosed sum. 

Now, the business employs about 150 people around the world, with a pack of them located in the New York headquarters, the company’s CEO, Farooq Malik, said in an interview last month.

The brand name Rain dawned on the founders because they saw how fast and fluid funds could be transferred using stablecoins. The same could be said for how quickly startup businesses are reacting to stablecoin developments, like the signing of the Genius Act, which created a regulatory framework for the digital assets.

President Donald Trump’s signing of that new law last year was pivotal in pushing the business forward, Malik said.

“The tipping point was really the Genius Act,” he said. “A lot of people had been waiting on the sidelines for clarity before proceeding. That gave companies and people the confidence to proceed. Consumers also have to believe this is viable.”

Now, the company aims to take another step in its evolution. It applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust charter this month, seeking the ability to offer asset custody and other related services, though they could still accept deposits or make loans. 

MassPay embraces stablecoins

Another startup growing in the stablecoin arena is Las Vegas-based MassPay, which is using the digital asset technology to streamline payments for gig workers, contractors and marketplace sellers as well as providing payout services for gaming and sports betting. It connects to local payment rails, real-time payment systems and mobile wallets.

“We've seen growing demand for stablecoins, primarily by large-scale institutions that feel comfortable due to some clearance in the regulation,” the company’s CEO, Ran Grushkowsky, said in an interview last month. Stablecoins are becoming particularly useful for speed and payments over the weekends, he explained.

The majority of MassPay’s 300 corporate clients are in North America, Grushkowsky said. They include Los Angeles-based online social platform Passes and New York-based marketplace Whop.

Last week, MassPay said it had forged a new integration with Block’s Cash App digital wallet.

MassPay’s services are offered in some 230 countries, according to the press release last December that named Grushkowsky CEO as of this year. The company has grown to process tens of billions of dollars annually, with about half of those payments moving across borders, and about 10% in stablecoins, he said.

The company is privately funded, and now employs about 54 workers, mainly in the U.S., Grushkowsky said. He declined to say how much money the owners have raised. 

As startups nudge stablecoins forward, the digital currency is slowly becoming a real possibility for payments in everyday life, Witt explained. 

“The biggest challenge, though, is that last mile of friction and localizing to consumer preferences,” Witt said. “We wanted to invest in the leaders around the world that are bridging the gap.”

title: FintechOS Elevate 2026: Can AI Deliver Beyond the Pilots and Promises?
snippet: FintechOS Elevate 2026 put AI's big promises to the test, from lending decisions and product innovation to the challenge of proving results. The post FintechOS Elevate 2026: Can AI Deliver Beyond the Pilots and Promises? appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The gap between AI ambition and real business results came under scrutiny at FintechOS Elevate 2026, as banking and insurance leaders discussed what it takes to turn investment in artificial intelligence into meaningful operational improvements.

Held at Kings Place in London on 14 October, the second annual Elevate conference attracted around 300 registrations and featured more than 25 speakers, with discussions spanning product innovation, customer experience, governance and the challenges of modernising financial services.

At last year’s Elevate, speakers warned against ‘AI theatre’ and pursuing projects without clear business objectives. Twelve months on, attention had turned to whether all that investment in AI was actually delivering results.

In her keynote, The AI Reckoning, author and board advisor Leda Glyptis challenged financial institutions to look beyond individual productivity gains and the growing number of AI pilots.

“Focus is a feature, not a bug,” she said, warning that poorly coordinated initiatives could introduce additional costs and operational risks.

Her message was that businesses need to measure improvements to their processes and outcomes, while addressing existing problems with data, skills and decision-making.

“If you want to be successful at your AI implementations, governance is your only friend,” she told the audience.

Leda Glyptis at FintechOS Elevate 2026

Bringing AI into everyday operations

FintechOS CEO and co-founder Teo Blidarus opened the conference by highlighting how fragmented products, workflows and data were preventing financial institutions from making full use of AI.

“Data fragmentation is typically a consequence of product fragmentation,” he said, explaining the need to connect products, data and workflows so AI can be used across everyday banking and insurance operations.

Blidarus also said FintechOS was introducing a new approach to implementation, after acknowledging that some customers had been “stuck in very complicated upgrades”.

A year after unveiling FintechOS 8 at Elevate 2025, the company introduced its latest release, FintechOS 8 Blue Sky, with new AI capabilities designed to support product development and everyday banking and insurance operations.

Blidarus and Byron Levin, head of presales and forward deployed consulting at FintechOS, demonstrated two AI copilots, Dex and Abi, built on the same agentic framework. Dex helps teams configure financial products, pricing, rules and workflows, while Abi supports employees and customers with day-to-day operations.

AI can help, but who makes the decisions?

In one demo, Abi guided a customer through a conversational loan application. Another used a fictional building society to show how AI could help develop and price mortgage products, assess broker applications and prepare commercial lending cases for review.

But the discussion also touched on how much decision-making should be left to AI.

“The lender, the bank, the financial institution has to own the decision,” said Joshua Weinstein, co-CEO of Gable Group, during a panel discussion on retail mortgage origination.

He warned that lenders still need to understand and explain how decisions are reached, even when AI has done much of the groundwork.

In the insurance sessions, FintechOS also demonstrated how AI could help with motor insurance pricing, claims, policy changes and payment reconciliation, with staff retaining responsibility for approving important decisions.

What does genuine transformation look like?

In the afternoon, Dharmesh Mistry, CEO of Vision 20/20 Consulting, challenged delegates to think about how AI might fundamentally change their businesses, rather than simply improve existing products and processes.

“It’s your own good numbers you have to be worried about,” he said. “Nokia had fantastic numbers. Kodak had fantastic numbers. Right until the quarter when they didn’t have good numbers.”

He reminded delegates that banks and insurers had adapted to the arrival of the internet and mobile technology, but suggested that several technologies advancing at once presented a different challenge.

“When technologies come alone, we adapt. When convergence comes, nobody’s got a framework for it because we didn’t imagine these several things coming together.”

Paroma Chatterjee chats to Teo Blidarus

Paroma Chatterjee, CEO of Revolut India, discussed how AI was becoming part of product development rather than something considered separately.

“We don’t look at AI as a different arm of the business,” she said, explaining how the company considered technology alongside licensing, local market requirements and customer needs when developing products.

But bringing AI into more parts of a business doesn’t necessarily mean better results. Rania Svoronou, global head of AI design at Citi, warned about the risk of building up ‘AI debt’ through multiple projects that improve individual customer interactions without making much difference to the overall experience.

title: Behind the Idea: Arf
snippet: Arf co-founder and CEO Ali Erhat Nalbant on why pre-funding still traps capital in cross-border payments and how on-demand settlement liquidity sets it free. The post Behind the Idea: Arf appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Cross-border payments are getting faster, but the capital behind them has not kept pace. Payment companies still pre-fund accounts across currencies and markets so that transactions can settle, leaving money idle that could otherwise go into hiring, better services or new markets.

Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and CEO at Arf

Arf, a Swiss-regulated financial institution, provides stablecoin-based settlement liquidity to licensed financial institutions, bridging fiat and stablecoin rails for B2B payment providers across the US, UK, EU, UAE, Hong Kong, Singapore and beyond.

In this Behind the Idea, Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and CEO of Arf, discusses the pre-funding problem the company was set up to solve, how its model has moved from direct lending to embedded infrastructure, and where it goes next.

Tell us more about your company and its offering

Arf is a Swiss-regulated global treasury platform providing liquidity and same-day settlement for international financial institutions. We enable international payments across fiat and stablecoin rails, offering IBANs, FX, and scalable treasury infrastructure.

As payments become faster, more global and increasingly real time, liquidity has become a major bottleneck. Innovations like faster rails and stablecoins are changing how money moves, but advances in speed cannot ultimately be realised if liquidity still determines when payments settle.

Our platform changes that by providing settlement liquidity, allowing financial institutions to support payment flows, enter new markets and scale without continually raising debt or diluting equity. We bridge fiat and stablecoins to deliver same-day liquidity to B2B payment providers, so their clients can access capital at the moment they need to send, rather than after a wire clears. Put simply, we help liquidity move as freely as payments, so our clients can grow faster while putting more of their own capital to work.

What problem was your company set up to solve?

We set up the company to solve a simple but persistent problem: payment businesses need liquidity exactly when demand appears, but traditional funding is often too slow, rigid and expensive. That means companies either hold excess capital that sits idle, which diverts capital away from company growth, whether that’s hiring, investing in better services or scaling to new markets, or they risk being caught short when payment volumes spike.

For decades, financial institutions have relied on prefunding accounts across currencies and markets to ensure liquidity is available wherever and whenever a payment needs to settle. Our aim is to make liquidity work more intelligently, by providing on-demand funding that can scale with real payment activity.

Ultimately, we want to ensure capital moves to where demand exists, when it is needed, so we can eliminate the trade-off between speed and capital efficiency in cross-border payments.

Since launch, how has your company evolved?

When we started Arf, the idea was simple: payment companies shouldn’t have to lock up capital just to guarantee they can settle. What’s evolved since then is the scale and sophistication of how we deliver that.

We’ve grown from serving individual financial institutions directly to embedding liquidity into the platforms and infrastructure they already use, so on-demand funding becomes part of their existing operations rather than a separate relationship to manage.

Today, we’ve processed more than $18bn in cumulative settlement with zero defaults across more than 1,400 days, tracked live on a public dashboard, not just reported internally. Our capital turns over 4.78 times per month, reflecting how actively our liquidity is being deployed across settlement flows.

What has been the biggest challenge or most ‘tricky moment’ to overcome?

One of the biggest challenges has been operating at the intersection of financial services, regulation, and new technology. Building a blockchain-based solution for a highly regulated industry required significant effort to establish the right regulatory and operational foundations, including becoming a regulated financial institution in Switzerland.

At the same time, demand has consistently been ahead of the capital available to us. We have had to learn how to make limited working capital work as efficiently as possible while continuously improving the model. Another challenge is that there is rarely a one-size-fits-all solution in cross-border payments. Every market and financial institution has its own requirements, which means we often have to solve problems individually and keep adapting as we scale.

What are your biggest achievements or ‘proudest moment’ so far?

I’m proud of how far we’ve scaled while staying focused on the core problem we set out to solve. We’ve now processed more than $18bn in cumulative settlement with zero defaults across more than 1,400 days. But beyond the numbers, I’m particularly proud of how this model has evolved from something transactional into real infrastructure.

We’re seeing partners across payments, stablecoin infrastructure and settlement networks build on top of what we’ve created, rather than simply using Arf as another financial service. That’s a meaningful shift for us.

How would you describe the culture of your company?

I would describe our culture as entrepreneurial, persistent, and deeply focused on solving real problems. We work on complex problems where there is rarely a simple, one-size-fits-all solution, so we stay very close to our customers and keep solving problems one by one.

There is also a strong culture of resilience. Building something new in financial infrastructure takes time, and there is always another challenge to solve and another piece to put in place. We are ambitious and excited about what we are building, but we also understand that progress comes from consistently doing the hard work. At the same time, we take regulation, compliance, and accountability very seriously because we are building infrastructure for the financial system.

What’s in store for the future?

Our focus is on scaling what we have built and making liquidity more accessible for financial institutions around the world. We see significant opportunities to expand into new markets, deepen our relationships with banks and financial institutions, and support more cross-border payment corridors, particularly in regions where prefunding still ties up the most working capital.

As the market continues to evolve, we want to keep building infrastructure that makes cross-border payments faster, more transparent, and more efficient. There is still a huge amount of liquidity trapped in traditional settlement processes, and our ambition is to play a meaningful role in changing that.

title: Three in Ten Brits say High Street Banks Worsened, CRIF Data Shows
snippet: CRIF's 2026 survey of 5,000 European consumers finds traditional banks are the only financial provider type with a negative service-quality net score. The post Three in Ten Brits say High Street Banks Worsened, CRIF Data Shows appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Traditional banks and building societies have become the only category of UK financial provider where consumers are more likely to say service has deteriorated than improved, according to research published on Tuesday by CRIF, the credit and decisioning analytics firm.

The findings draw on a survey of 5,000 consumers across five European markets conducted by Opinium Research between March and April 2026. In the UK, 29% of respondents said service from high street banks and building societies had worsened over the past three years, against 26% who said it had improved, yielding a net score of negative three. Digital banks and fintechs recorded a net score of positive 36, with 43% of respondents citing improvement and only 7% citing deterioration.

The service gap in numbers

Sara Costantini, regional director for the UK and Ireland at CRIF

The table from the CRIF report illustrates a clear hierarchy. Investment and asset management firms scored a net positive 12, credit and lending providers positive nine, and insurers flat. Traditional incumbents stood alone in negative territory. Sara Costantini, regional director for the UK and Ireland at CRIF, said incumbents can no longer rely on scale or legacy to retain customers: “Digital banks and fintechs are setting the standard for what good looks like in financial services, and consumers can see the difference.”

Branch closures are a contributing factor. One in five respondents (20%) said that the reduction in physical branches had made it harder to access support, while 16% said the growth of digital services had itself reduced service quality and 15% believed digitisation had been driven primarily by cost reduction rather than customer benefit. That last figure matters commercially: it suggests a meaningful segment of consumers is sceptical of digital migration as a service improvement rather than a cost exercise.

Despite this ambivalence, adoption of digital-only accounts is accelerating. Separate data cited by CRIF, sourced from Finder, shows that 49% of UK consumers had opened a digital-only bank account by 2026, up from 40% in 2025 and 36% in 2024. The trajectory suggests that negative sentiment about incumbent service quality has not slowed account migration.

Competitive and regulatory context

The findings land at a difficult moment for the major UK retail banks. Branch closure programmes across Lloyds Banking Group, NatWest and Barclays have continued through 2025 and 2026, drawing scrutiny from the FCA and the Treasury Select Committee over access to cash and in-person services. The regulator’s Consumer Duty rules, which came fully into force in 2023, place explicit obligations on firms to demonstrate good outcomes for all customer segments, including those who cannot or will not use digital channels. A persistent negative net service score creates a paper trail that compliance teams will need to address.

For the challenger banks, the CRIF data provides further validation of the positioning that firms such as Monzo, Starling and Revolut have built their growth strategies around. Customer satisfaction has been a primary competitive differentiator rather than product breadth, and the gap shown here reinforces that advantage. The strategic question for challengers is whether a positive service perception can translate into primary banking relationships and the deposit balances and lending volumes that accompany them.

Costantini framed the challenge for incumbents as a dual mandate: “The banks that will win out are those that match the challengers on digital experience without leaving behind the people who relied on in-person services. Customers do not choose between digital and human banking. They expect both.”

The research forms part of CRIF’s 2026 Banking on Banks report series. A second report, due later in October, will examine the financial services gap between consumers and businesses.

Victims of a £1.5m crypto investment fraud will recover lost funds after the FCA obtained confiscation orders against Raymondip Bedi and Patrick Mavanga.

title: Fed names new payments chief
snippet: Federal Reserve Financial Services tapped Kim Robbins to succeed Mark Gould starting in November.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve’s financial services division has appointed Kim Robbins as its new top payments executive, tapping her to replace the retiring Mark Gould.

Federal Reserve Financial Services announced the appointment Thursday, picking a nearly 20-year Federal Reserve veteran to lead the division that provides payments services to financial institutions. She’ll step into the role on Nov. 16, according to the press release stating her appointment.

She has served as first vice president and chief operating officer at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City since March 2024 and has been with that reserve bank in some capacity since January 2012, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to heading to that regional bank, she worked for Federal Reserve Financial Services as the chief of enterprise services.

In a post last week on that social media site, Robbins said she was pleased to “return ‘home’ to payments.” She also gave a nod to the work that lies ahead.

“With rapid innovation transforming the industry, it is clear to me that we are in a pivotal moment in payments,” she said. “I look forward to partnering across the Federal Reserve System and with our industry stakeholders to advance modern, secure, and resilient payment services that meet the dynamic and evolving needs of financial institutions, businesses, and the American public.”

Gould is retiring after spending the last three years with a key focus on rolling out the Fed’s instant payments system FedNow, starting in mid 2023, and trying to lure banks across the country to join the system. As of this month, the central bank has attracted just over 1,900 U.S. banks and credit unions to use the real-time payments system.

With some 8,500 financial institutions in the U.S. eligible to use the system, the Fed has a ways to go in drawing more banks and credit unions to the new service. Last month, the Fed began offering a discount program to entice financial institutions to participate in the service.

Only U.S. financial institutions can join the system, which enables them to send payments in a matter of seconds or minutes, as opposed to transactions sometimes taking days to settle. The Fed launched the instant payments system in July 2023 in the hopes of bringing smaller banks into the realm of faster payments. That followed the start of a private real-time system, the RTP Network, by bigger banks that own The Clearing House in November 2017.

In late 2024, the Fed disclosed that it cost about $246 million to operate the FedNow payments system that year, after requiring about $100 million for development in 2023, according to a report from the central bank. 

The central bank this year has also been exploring how to extend the reach of the system across international borders. Last month, the Fed said the real-time system was “on the verge” of providing cross-border transaction “support,” but then it stopped short of saying how and when. 

Robbins has leadership experience both with respect to FedNow as well as the broader Federal Reserve Financial Services, the release said. 

Specifically, the release noted that she was FedNow’s chief administrative officer, leading the “functions supporting the program’s rapid scale-up across multiple Federal Reserve Banks,” plus “strengthening the governance, risk, compliance and legal structures” for the system.

Aside from FedNow, Robbins will oversee the Fed’s retail, wholesale and securities services for financial institutions, the release noted.

Before Robbins joined the Fed, she had an early start to her career in a different kind of retail sector. She worked for seven years for the GAP and Payless ShoeSource, managing various aspects of the retail chains’ business lines.

title: Emirates NBD Opens VIP SME Programme to All Business Banking Clients
snippet: Emirates NBD is broadening its invitation-only VIP Privilege Program to all eligible Business Banking customers in the UAE, anchored by a new Visa Infinite The post Emirates NBD Opens VIP SME Programme to All Business Banking Clients appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Emirates NBD has expanded its VIP Privilege Program for Business Banking clients, widening access from an invitation-only arrangement to all existing business customers and new customers within qualifying packages. The Dubai-headquartered bank announced the move on 7 October 2026, framing it as a structural upgrade to its premium SME proposition in the UAE.

The programme operates on a points-based qualification model. Business Banking clients must accumulate 100,000 points in a review year, generated through deposits, loan and wealth balances, and transaction volumes in foreign exchange and trade finance. Customers on the bank’s Emirati package receive a 25% bonus on qualifying points, a concession that reflects the UAE’s broader policy emphasis on supporting national-owned enterprises.

What the programme delivers

At the centre of the offering sits the Visa Infinite Business Debit Card, which Emirates NBD describes as a first of its kind for a business debit product in the MENA region. The card anchors a wider suite of services, including direct-to-agent contact centre access with no queue, priority handling at Business Banking Centres, a dedicated relationship manager, and preferential pricing on banking fees.

Beyond the core banking relationship, the programme extends into operational savings. Members receive discounts on airport meet-and-assist services across more than 450 global destinations, preferred car rental rates, and access to reduced pricing on marketing tools, HR and finance software, co-working space rentals and business publications. Lifestyle perks include complimentary access to more than 1,000 airport lounges globally, concierge support for dining and travel, and valet parking at major UAE landmarks.

Hamad Mohamed Zayed, group head of business banking at Emirates NBD, said: “This initiative recognises the vital role of businesses in economic growth and provides them with preferential pricing and curated privileges that add tangible value to both their daily business operations and personal lifestyle.”

Market context

The structured bundling of banking services, operational tools and lifestyle benefits for SMEs is a segment that several Gulf banks have moved into as they compete for the primary banking relationship with the region’s growing cohort of small and mid-sized firms. Emirates NBD’s scale, with AED 1.3 trillion in total assets as at June 2026 and a network spanning 13 countries, gives it distribution depth that most challenger propositions in the region cannot match.

The qualifying mechanics matter here. Tying VIP status to deposit, loan, wealth and FX balances rather than to a flat fee is a deliberate design to deepen primary banking relationships rather than simply reward card spend. It creates a consolidation incentive: the more of a business’s banking activity sits with Emirates NBD, the easier it is to reach the 100,000-point threshold. This approach is consistent with a broader trend among incumbent banks in the Gulf to use loyalty architecture as a defensive tool against both regional competitors and the growing presence of digital business banking platforms.

The regulatory environment in the UAE, overseen by the Central Bank of the UAE under its Financial Infrastructure Transformation programme, has been pushing for greater SME financial access and digital service delivery. A programme that combines preferential pricing with digital channel integration through the businessONLINE platform aligns with that policy direction, even if the release frames it primarily in commercial terms.

The next meaningful disclosure to watch is uptake data: the number of qualifying customers in the first review year and the proportion of the bank’s SME base that reaches the 100,000-point threshold will indicate whether the programme is genuinely broadening access or functioning as a retention tool for a narrow top tier.

title: Ant International and HSBC Extend Tokenised Deposits to Middle East
snippet: The pair have completed pilot treasury transactions across UAE corridors, making Ant International HSBC's first Middle East client for its Tokenised Deposit Service. The post Ant International and HSBC Extend Tokenised Deposits to Middle East appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Ant International has expanded its real-time treasury management operations into the Middle East through an enlarged collaboration with HSBC, completing pilot transactions across two UAE-anchored payment corridors. The milestone makes Ant International the first client in the region to use HSBC’s Tokenised Deposit Service (TDS).

The two corridors tested were intra-UAE dirham transfers executed in real time within the UAE, and cross-border US dollar payments initiated from the UAE and settled with counterparties in Hong Kong and Singapore. Both sets of transactions were initiated through WhaleRTP, Ant International’s proprietary blockchain-based treasury platform, and executed via HSBC’s TDS. The workflow was jointly designed by both institutions.

The infrastructure at play

Kyle Boag, regional head of global payments solutions for the MENAT region at HSBC

WhaleRTP is not a new product. Ant International has operated blockchain-based treasury infrastructure since 2019, deploying it across major financial centres including Hong Kong, Singapore, Europe and the United States. The platform is currently connected to more than 20 global banking partners and handles real-time transfers in over 17 currencies, including the US dollar, Hong Kong dollar and UAE dirham. The Middle East expansion represents a geographic extension of an established operational layer rather than a greenfield technology deployment.

Kelvin Li, general manager of platform tech and senior vice president at Ant International

HSBC’s TDS, meanwhile, is now live in six markets: Hong Kong, Singapore, Luxembourg, the UK, the United States and the UAE. It supports seven currencies, including the Chinese offshore renminbi, euro, pound sterling and dirham. Kyle Boag, HSBC’s regional head of global payments solutions for the MENAT region, said the service demonstrates “interoperability between tokenised deposit networks,” adding that for corporate clients the practical benefit is the ability to move liquidity across markets and financial institutions with improved cash visibility.

Kelvin Li, general manager of platform tech and senior vice president at Ant International, framed the move as a step toward establishing “a global treasury hub in the Middle East,” a commercially significant ambition given the region’s growing role in cross-border trade and digital finance investment. Ant International’s operational footprint in the Gulf includes Alipay+, its merchant payments network, Antom, its payment gateway business, and WorldFirst, its cross-border payments platform for small and medium enterprises.

Regulatory and market context

The expansion sits at an intersection that regulators in the Gulf are actively developing. The UAE’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority and the Dubai Financial Services Authority have both issued frameworks covering digital asset activity, and the Abu Dhabi Global Market has separately been working to attract institutional blockchain infrastructure. Tokenised deposits, which represent commercial bank money on a distributed ledger rather than a new currency or a stablecoin, sit in a cleaner regulatory category and do not require the same licensing as a digital asset exchange or a virtual asset service provider. That distinction is meaningful for corporates with conservative treasury mandates.

More broadly, institutional tokenised deposit infrastructure is gaining traction as a mechanism for solving practical cash-management problems, particularly 24/7 liquidity access and the ability to settle across time zones without the credit and settlement risk associated with correspondent banking chains. HSBC joins JPMorgan, Citi and Standard Chartered in operating live tokenised deposit or intraday liquidity networks, though the specific currency and geography coverage differs across each platform. The competitive question for the HSBC and Ant International partnership is whether the joint workflow can attract third-party corporate clients beyond Ant International’s own affiliates, and whether the dirham corridor becomes a template for further Gulf Cooperation Council currencies.

title: Upgrade applies for ILC charter
snippet: The decade-old credit-card startup named a SoFi alum and longtime regulator as CEO of its proposed bank.
fullText:
Upgrade has applied for an industrial loan company charter with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Nevada Financial Institutions Division, the fintech announced Monday.

“We are excited at the prospect of establishing a new bank that will advance Upgrade’s mission of bringing responsible and affordable credit to consumers,” Virginia Varela, proposed CEO of Upgrade Bank, said in a statement. 

Varela brings more than 40 years of experience in the banking sector – first, as a regulator. She spent more than two decades with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and another two years as a senior bank examiner with the Federal Reserve, before specializing in bank turnarounds after the 2007-08 financial crisis, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Varela was CEO of Sacramento, California-based Golden Pacific Bank when SoFi bought the lender. She became head of SoFi’s community banking unit but left in July 2025 for Upgrade, where she is head of banking strategy.

Varela will serve on Upgrade Bank’s board alongside Upgrade co-founder and CFO Jeffrey Bogan, the company said. Raymond Specht, onetime CEO of Toyota Financial Savings Bank, will serve as an independent director on the board.

Upgrade launched roughly a decade ago offering personal loans but gradually expanded to encompass credit cards, mobile banking, auto financing and buy now, pay later. The fintech has delivered about $53 billion in credit to roughly 8.5 million customers, it said.

Upgrade counts Cross River and Celtic Bank as partners on loans, credit lines and banking services. An ILC charter would make Upgrade less dependent on those relationships.

Trump-era regulators have seen a sharp increase in new charter applications. FDIC Chair Travis Hill last year touted the ILC charter as one of a handful of ways to boost the establishment of new banks.

Rent fintech Flex and BNPL juggernaut Klarna Group applied for ILC charters in July. Car maker Stellantis received approval in May to launch an ILC. Other automotive stalwarts, including Ford and General Motors, got green lights in January. Investment firm Edward Jones followed in February. 

Some lawmakers, with backing from the banking industry, have argued that an ILC charter exempts companies from the definition of a “bank” under the Bank Holding Company Act. As long as ILCs don’t offer demand deposit accounts, they can bypass oversight by the Federal Reserve, the politicians contend.

The trade group Independent Community Bankers of America said in May that cutting the Fed out of ILC supervision “leav[es] a dangerous gap in safety and soundness oversight and introducing unnecessary systemic risk into the banking system.”

Last year, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-MA, and Andy Kim, D-NJ, proposed a moratorium on commercially owned ILC charters until such entities are defined as “banks” under the BHC Act.

title: Businesses view stablecoins warily
snippet: Despite the hype surrounding the digital assets, businesses remain cool to using the cryptocurrency, according to the results of a Cleveland Federal Reserve survey.
fullText:
Stablecoins aren’t going to become a disruptive force in payments in the United States anytime soon as businesses are displaying a lack of enthusiasm for the digital currency, based on a survey by the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank.

Reasons businesses are cool to using stablecoins include lack of familiarity with the technology; satisfaction with legacy payment options; and little to no demand among customers and suppliers to use stablecoins for payment, according to the results of the Cleveland Fed’s survey in late September.

Of the survey’s 148 respondents, only one said it is currently using stablecoins. Among the remaining respondents, seven said they plan to use stablecoins in the future. The other respondents either said they weren’t sure they would use stablecoins in the future or expressed a lack of familiarity with the digital currency.

The results were somewhat surprising to Federal Reserve researchers conducting the survey as they expected more respondents to have plans to begin using stablecoins. 

“We didn’t expect the results to be as lopsided as they were,” Peter Zimmerman, a research economist for the Cleveland Fed who co-authored the report, said in summarizing the survey’s results during an interview earlier this month. 

Lack of knowledge about stablecoins is a big reason why businesses are not rushing to accept them for payment or use stablecoins for payment, according to the Cleveland Fed’s report. 

When asked what factors would influence their decision to use stablecoins, 49 respondents, about a third, cited the need for more time to observe market trends and adoption. 

While respondents were not “terribly critical” of stablecoins in their comments, many said they needed “more time to understand the technology,” Zimmerman said.

The Federal Reserve of Cleveland conducted its research in September 2025, about two months after the Genius Act became law, providing a federal regulatory framework for stablecoin payments. The Federal Reserve of Cleveland surveyed companies in the Fourth Federal Reserve District, which includes Ohio, western Pennsylvania, eastern Kentucky, and the northern panhandle of West Virginia.

One reason businesses may lack knowledge about stablecoins and potential use cases for the digital currency is that they are primarily being used for back-end settlement between banks, which keeps the technology in the background.

“What we are seeing is stablecoins being linked to cards for payments, which on the front end looks like a normal card transaction,” said Aaron McPherson, principal of AFM Consulting, in an interview this month. “Banks settle those transactions in stablecoins on the back-end between themselves, but the public doesn’t see that. What they see is the front-end of the transaction.”

Another roadblock to stablecoins becoming a mainstream payment option is the efficiency, cost effectiveness and competitiveness of existing payment options in the U.S., such as the ACH network. Some 42 survey respondents, just under a third of those surveyed, said they need more evidence stablecoins are cheaper or more efficient than other forms of payment.

“Any new payment option clearly has to be better than the existing options to break the inertia,” McPherson said. “There is a cost of acceptance for stablecoins, like other payment options, but stablecoins don’t have a clear economic advantage over many established payment methods yet.”

Lack of demand from customers to pay with stablecoins is also a barrier for businesses to accept or pay with stablecoins. Among respondents to the Cleveland Fed’s survey, 50, or about a third, said consumer demand to accept stablecoins for payment is a key factor influencing their decision to use stablecoins.

“To get people to want to pay with stablecoins, they need an inducement to do so, such as earning rewards,” McPherson said.

McPherson likens the situation to the chicken and egg scenario with any new payment option: acceptance drives usage and vice versa. “Inducing demand to spend stablecoins will boost acceptance,” McPherson added.

Despite the many headwinds facing stablecoins as a payment option, the best use case for the digital currency is cross-border payments, say some industry consultants. Using stablecoins for cross-border payments enables funds to move directly between the sender’s and recipient’s digital wallet, which reduces the number of parties involved in the transaction, lowers fees and speeds the transaction.

“In the U.S., stablecoins are largely a niche payment option and their best use case is cross-border payments,” Tony DeSanctis, vice president for Cornerstone Advisors, said in an interview this month. “Businesses that have a lot of international clients is where we will see activity.”

If businesses are going to overcome their lack of enthusiasm for using stablecoins, they need an answer to the question of how stablecoins will improve operations.

“Businesses need to be educated about what the technology is capable of, [to understand] whether it can disrupt the current state of payments and find the niche where it can serve,” DeSanctis said. “No one knows for sure what technology will be the next market disruptor, but we haven’t seen enough of stablecoins to make that distinction.”

The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'
